newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court rejects evidence against Thai banker.
newsitem.headline: Canada court rejects evidence against Thai banker.

text.p: A Canadian judge presiding over an extradition hearing for a former Thai bank official accused of embezzlement ruled on Monday that some prosecution evidence was hearsay and not admissible in court.

The ruling by British Columbia Supreme Court Justice Frank Maczko was a setback for the prosecution's case against Rakesh Saxena, the former treasury advisor for the Bangkok Bank of Commerce who is charged in Thailand with embezzling about $65 million from the bank.
Saxena, an Indian citizen and former resident of Thailand, was arrested last year by Canadian and Thai police at the Whistler mountain resort neat Vancouver.

Monday's decision threw out testimony by two witnesses against Saxena contained in affidavits obtained by Thai police. Canadian federal prosecutor Deborah Strachan, who is representing Thai authorities in the extradition case, declined to comment on the impact of the ruling.

The prosecution has attempted to demonstrate that Saxena and a group of bank executives arranged for the Bangkok bank to loan $65 million to private firms, including City Trading Corp., that were controlled by Saxena.
But the judge ruled that statements by an employee of one of the firms failed to establish that Saxena controlled them and should not be considered.

He also ruled that statements by a bank auditor about loans to City Trading Corp. were not supported by bank documents and thus not admissible as evidence. Although the prosecution concluded its case on Monday, the court said loan documents would be accepted as evidence later if the prosecution were to submit them during the hearing.
Saxena's lawyer, Winton Derby, said he expected to submit on Tuesday defense evidence that included a constitutional challenge.

The week-old extradition hearing was initially expected to conclude this week but Strachan said the presentation of Saxena's defense appeared likely to prolong proceedings past Friday. That would force a delay until September because the judge will not be available again until then.
The Thai government took over the Bangkok bank a year ago after a public run on deposits sparked by news it was saddled with about $2.7 billion in bad loans.
